headline: Bunker Balled Up on Stratford Shoal — Blues Slashing, Bass Waiting on Dark
subhead: Peanut bunker packed the mouth of the Sound this week, and the thermal wall at Stratford Shoal is sorting who gets to eat first.
body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning just watching before I ever made a cast. Off the Port Jeff breakwater, a bait ball of peanut bunker the size of a swimming pool was pinned against the rocks by the outgoing tide, and there wasn't a bird in the sky touching it — which told me more than any temp gauge could. Something bigger was already underneath, holding them tight instead of letting terns scatter them. Fifteen minutes later a school of bluefish came through like a lawnmower, and that bait ball just disappeared into white water and feathers. That's the story of Central Sound this week: the bunker are here in numbers, and everybody's lined up to eat them, just not all at the same hour.

The thermal picture explains a lot of the behavior I'm seeing. Kings Point is sitting around 72 degrees, New London's still holding near 70, and that gradient means the warmer water piling up toward our end of the Sound is stacking bait and holding it — bunker, mullet, silversides, all funneling through the narrows between the Norwalk Islands and Port Jeff because that's where the Sound squeezes down and the current does the sorting for them. Predators know it too. It's why Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground Light keep producing even when the open basin looks quiet.

Bluefish are the daylight story right now. With bunker schools pushing along the shoreline from the Norwalk Islands up toward Charles Island, blues are blitzing right on the surface in broad daylight — something you don't always get once July water warms up this much. I watched three separate blitzes this week between Sheffield Island and Charles Island, all within two hours of the top of the tide. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — worked fine when you could get in range, but the bigger blues (four to six pounds, a few bigger) wanted something slower once the top-water frenzy broke up. Diamond jigs bounced just under the surface picked off stragglers after the schools sounded.

Striped bass have gone the other way. With surface water running into the mid-to-upper 70s through the day, the bass have pulled back into a low-light program — first light, last light, and after dark around bunker schools and current edges. Stratford Shoal rip is still the best bet for this, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when bait gets funneled off the shoal into deeper water. Eels drifted along bottom, and bucktails worked slow with a Gulp trailer, have been taking slot fish in the 28-34 inch range after dark. A few boats working the Norwalk Islands after sundown are finding better numbers than size — lots of schoolies mixed with the occasional overslot that comes up out of nowhere on a bunker chunk.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing going, and it hasn't blinked with the heat the way stripers have. Structure and moving water are still the formula — the edges around Middle Ground Light, the rockpiles off Charles Island, and the deeper cuts through the Norwalk Islands are holding fish through the tide changes. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift in 25 to 40 feet, have been the go-to. Keeper-sized fish to five pounds have shown up consistently, with a decent short-to-keeper ratio — you're not culling all day, but you're not getting skunked either.

Porgies are stacking up thick on the reef structure around the Norwalk Islands and the rockier stretches off Charles Island. Sandworms and clam on a high-low rig, bottom fished on the last of the incoming, has been about as close to a sure thing as this Sound offers right now. Nothing glamorous, but good eating and steady rods.

Weakfish have been a quieter presence, mostly showing in the back-bay mud around Oyster Bay and the Huntington side on the tail end of the ebb, when the shallow water warms fastest and pushes bait out through the creek mouths. Legal fish are mixed in with the fluke crowd there — not a targeted bite yet, more of a bonus.

We've had our eye on the bonito question since bait started concentrating through the narrows, and I haven't seen a confirmed fish push into Central Sound yet — but the ingredients are lining up. Rain bait and grass shrimp have been thick around the Norwalk Islands, and that's exactly the kind of forage that pulls bonito in behind it once water conditions settle. I'd keep a small metal rigged on a rod and watch the surface around Charles Island and the outer islands over the next week or two.

Looking ahead, we're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which should slacken the current at Stratford Shoal and the other rip-dependent spots. That's not bad news — it widens the productive window past the peak of the tide for eel and swimbait presentations, so you won't be chained to the exact top of the flood or ebb to get bit. If the bunker schools hold their pattern through the narrows, I'd fish the last light window at Stratford Shoal for bass, work the Norwalk Islands blitzes for blues during the day, and keep the fluke rods rigged on the structure edges regardless — that part of the program hasn't needed fixing.
